title: Conditional sentences

objectives.can: Recognise a condition with אִם, כִּי, לוּ or no particle at all, and say what it supposes.

explanation.summary: A conditional sentence has two parts: the condition (the 'if' clause) and the answer to it. Hebrew marks the condition with אִם, כִּי or לוּ, and sometimes with no particle at all. The verb forms do not by themselves say how likely the condition is, so a reader must weigh the particle, the verb and the context together.

sections.heading: The two parts
body: Grammarians call the condition the protasis and the answer the apodosis. In English, 'if you do well (protasis), you will be accepted (apodosis)'. The protasis comes first in Hebrew as in English, and the apodosis follows, often joined to it with a וְ or with no link at all.

The verb forms vary. A protasis may have a yiqtol, a qatal, a participle or no verb. The apodosis may have a yiqtol, a weqatal, an imperative, a nominal clause or a qatal. The forms do not by themselves tell you how likely the supposed event is. They show it by the way they are used in a given place, as Hebrew has few devices that stand for English 'would' and 'had'.

sections.heading: אִם: the usual 'if'
body: אִם is the commonest particle of condition. It supposes something that may or may not be: 'if I have found favour' (it is left open), 'if he enters alone' (it may happen). It often takes a yiqtol when the event lies ahead, and a qatal when it lies behind or is thought of as complete, and it can stand before a noun or a phrase where the verb is understood.
A negative condition is אִם לֹא, 'if not'. Do not confuse it with the oath use described below, in which the same two words mean something else.
אִם often introduces alternatives side by side: 'if you do well … and if you do not do well …'. A speaker can in this way put two sides of one choice.

sections.heading: כִּי in the laws, and אִם for the sub-cases
body: כִּי has many uses (it can mean 'that', 'because', 'when', 'for'), and one of them is 'if' or 'when'. In the collections of laws this is a pattern worth watching. The main case is introduced by כִּי, and the sub-cases, which depend on it, by אִם: 'When a man buys a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years; if he came in alone, he shall go out alone; if he had a wife, …' (this is the order of Exodus 21:2–4). Leviticus 1 has the same pattern, with a general case after כִּי and the particular offerings after אִם.

That is a tendency of the legal style, not a rule; a new main case may also begin with וְכִי, and the two particles are sometimes mixed in the same law. The pattern helps a reader to see the structure of a long law.

sections.heading: לוּ and לוּלֵי: what is contrary to fact, and wishes
body: לוּ supposes something that is not so, or not yet so, or is only hoped for. With it two meanings are common. One is the wish: 'if only …', with the verb in the qatal or yiqtol. The other is the contrary-to-fact condition, 'if it had been so …', where the answer says what would have followed. The context shows which is meant.

לוּלֵי means 'if it had not been for …' and takes a noun or a clause. It speaks of something that was in fact the case and says what would have happened without it. Genesis 31:42 is the clearest example in the Torah.

sections.heading: Conditions with no particle, and oaths
body: Two clauses placed side by side may stand as condition and answer. The condition has no 'if'. A weqatal or a qatal first and a weqatal after it may mean 'if he leaves, he will die'. An imperative followed by וְ and a form that states the result means 'do this, and (then) you will live'. The reader sees the condition from the logic, not from a particle.

In an oath, אִם works by a different logic. The speaker swears by something and then states the thing sworn about in the form of an unfinished condition: 'as you live, if I do this …' The consequence of failure is left unsaid. Such a clause means 'I will not do this'. The negative אִם לֹא, 'if I do not …', in the same pattern means the opposite: 'surely I will'. These meanings are found where the oath is complete and where it is only implied.

misunderstandings: The verb form does not tell you how real the condition is. A qatal after אִם is not a past tense 'if he had …'. It can stand for an event that has already come about (as in 'if I have found favour') and the English may need 'has'.
אִם לֹא does not always mean 'if not'. In an oath it means 'surely'.
כִּי does not always mean 'because'. In laws and general statements it often means 'if' or 'when'.
Without an 'if' word, a pair of clauses may still be a condition. Do not look for a particle in every case.

deeper.heading: 'If' or 'even if'?
body: Some verses with אִם are read as concessive: 'even if', 'though'. In Job 9:20 the clause with אִם אֶצְדָּק can be read as an open condition, 'if I am in the right, my mouth will condemn me', or as a concession, 'even if I am in the right …'. The Hebrew allows both, and each reading fits the speaker's complaint. The difference is a difference of translation, and it does not change the form of the clause. The grammar does not decide between the two; the reader weighs the context.

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: If thou buy a Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve; and in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The main case of the law on Hebrew slaves is introduced by כִּי with a yiqtol: 'when you buy …'. The answer, with another yiqtol, says what the law provides: six years he shall serve. The particle does not mean 'because' here; it opens the case.

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: If he come in by himself, he shall go out by himself; if he be married, then his wife shall go out with him.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two sub-cases follow the main case, each introduced by אִם. The first has a yiqtol in both parts, the condition (he comes in alone) and the answer (he goes out alone). The second condition is a nominal clause: if he is a married man, then, with a weqatal, his wife shall go out with him.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And we said unto my lord: The lad cannot leave his father; for if he should leave his father, his father would die.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: No particle marks the condition. The two weqatal verbs וְעָזַב and וָמֵת, set side by side, mean 'if he leaves his father, (then) he will die': the first clause names the case and the second what follows. The speaker, Judah, says it of a possible event, not of something that has happened.

quoted.title: 2 Samuel
quoted.english: And Uriah said unto David: 'The ark, and Israel, and Judah, abide in booths; and my lord Joab, and the servants of my lord, are encamped in the open field; shall I then go into my house, to eat and to drink, and to lie with my wife? as thou livest, and as thy soul liveth, I will not do this thing.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: An oath. After the formula 'as you live and as your soul lives' comes אִם with a yiqtol. The clause is left without its consequence, and the whole means a strong denial: 'I will not do this thing'. The negative reading is the usual sense of אִם after an oath.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Except the God of my father, the God of Abraham, and the Fear of Isaac, had been on my side, surely now hadst thou sent me away empty. God hath seen mine affliction and the labour of my hands, and gave judgment yesternight.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: לוּלֵי names a fact: the God of the speaker's father was on his side. The answer says what would have happened without it, 'surely now you would have sent me away empty'. The sentence speaks of what in fact did not happen. A real condition would use אִם.

practice.prompt: What does וְכִי־ (word 0) do at the head of this law?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: And if a man sell his daughter to be a maid-servant, she shall not go out as the men-servants do.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It introduces a wish
It introduces a quotation, 'that'
It introduces a new case of the law: 'and if a man sells his daughter …'
It introduces a reason, 'because'
practice.explain: In the laws of Exodus 21, כִּי opens a case. The verse takes up a new case with וְכִי, and its answer follows, 'she shall not go out as the men-servants do'.

practice.prompt: What does לוּ־ (word 12) mean in this verse?

quoted.title: Numbers
quoted.english: And all the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron; and the whole congregation said unto them: 'Would that we had died in the land of Egypt! or would we had died in this wilderness!
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A wish: 'if only we had died …'
A reason: 'because we died'
A command: 'die!'
A real condition: 'if we have died'
practice.explain: The people are not supposing a fact but wishing it had happened. The qatal מַתְנוּ after לוּ expresses a wish about the past. The sense is 'would that we had died'.

practice.prompt: What kind of condition is לוּ חָפֵץ יְהוָה לַהֲמִיתֵנוּ (words 3 to 6), with the answer in the words after it?

quoted.title: Judges
quoted.english: But his wife said unto him: 'If the LORD were pleased to kill us, He would not have received a burnt-offering and a meal-offering at our hand, neither would He have shown us all these things, nor would at this time have told such things as these.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: An open condition: the speaker does not know whether the LORD wished to kill them
A condition contrary to fact: the LORD did not wish to kill them, as the answer shows
A command
An oath
practice.explain: The answer says that in that case the LORD would not have accepted their offering nor shown them these things. He did accept it and show them, so the supposition is false. Hence לוּ, 'if it had been so'.

practice.prompt: How is the condition expressed in עֲשׂוּ וִחְיוּ (words 6 and 7)?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Joseph said unto them the third day. 'This do, and live; for I fear God:
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: By the particle אִם
By no particle: an imperative followed by וְ and a form giving the result, 'do this and live'
By the particle כִּי
By a form of לוּ
practice.explain: The command and its consequence are set side by side. The sense is 'if you do this, you will live'. A conditional reading is clear without a particle, as the result clause follows the command.

practice.prompt: How does the clause beginning וְאִם־ (word 0) stand to the case before it?

quoted.title: Leviticus
quoted.english: And if his offering be of the flock, whether of the sheep, or of the goats, for a burnt-offering, he shall offer it a male without blemish.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It is a reason for the case before it
It is a different case of the same law: an offering from the flock instead of the herd
It is a question
It is a wish
practice.explain: Leviticus 1 sets out the offerings by their kinds. The earlier verse is about the herd, and this one takes up the flock. Sub-cases are commonly introduced by אִם.

check.prompt: What does the clause אִם נָא מָצָאתִי חֵן בְּעֵינֶיךָ (words 2 to 6) suppose?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: and said: 'My lord, if now I have found favour in thy sight, pass not away, I pray thee, from thy servant.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: An open condition with a qatal: 'if I have found favour', left to the hearer
An oath
Something contrary to fact
A wish about the past
check.explain: The speaker does not say that he has found favour; he leaves it open. The qatal looks at the event as complete, and the answer is an appeal, אַל נָא תַעֲבֹר, 'do not pass by'.

check.prompt: What form does the answer (apodosis) take in this law?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: If a thief be found breaking in, and be smitten so that he dieth, there shall be no bloodguiltiness for him.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A command
A qatal
A wish
A nominal clause, אֵין לוֹ דָּמִים, 'there is no bloodguilt for him'
check.explain: The condition is introduced by אִם with a niphal yiqtol, and two weqatals continue it. The answer is a clause with no verb, built on אֵין. The answer need not repeat the verb form of the condition.

check.prompt: What does אִם mean in וְאִם אֶקַּח (words 5 and 6), after the oath of the verse before?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: that I will not take a thread nor a shoe-latchet nor aught that is thine, lest thou shouldest say: I have made Abram rich;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It marks a wish
It makes the statement a denial: 'I will not take', the unfinished oath form
It marks a reason
It supposes something that may happen: 'if I take'
check.explain: Abram has just sworn, in the verse before, and אִם in an oath means 'not'. The words say that he will take nothing from the king of Sodom, even a thread or a sandal strap.

check.prompt: What does אִם־לֹא (words 16 and 17) mean in this speech of the Aramean servants?

quoted.title: 1 Kings
quoted.english: And the servants of the king of Aram said unto him: 'Their God is a God of the hills; therefore they were stronger than we; but let us fight against them in the plain, and surely we shall be stronger than they.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: 'If not': an open condition
'Because not'
'Surely': the form of an oath, with the consequence left unsaid
'Although not'
check.explain: The servants are not weighing a possibility. They declare that their own side will be stronger, and grammarians explain the form as an oath with its consequence left unsaid. The negative אִם לֹא in that pattern means 'surely'.

check.prompt: What does לוּלֵי (word 0) say about the God of Jacob's father?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Except the God of my father, the God of Abraham, and the Fear of Isaac, had been on my side, surely now hadst thou sent me away empty. God hath seen mine affliction and the labour of my hands, and gave judgment yesternight.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It supposes that he was absent and says what then would have been; in fact he was present
It is a wish that he were present
It is an oath by him
It is a question about him
check.explain: 'If it had not been for the God of my father …' tells that he was on Jacob's side. The answer states the result that did not take place, 'surely now you would have sent me away empty'.

check.prompt: How does the clause אִם עֹלָה קָרְבָּנוֹ מִן הַבָּקָר (words 0 to 4) stand to the verse before it?

quoted.title: Leviticus
quoted.english: If his offering be a burnt-offering of the herd, he shall offer it a male without blemish; he shall bring it to the door of the tent of meeting, that he may be accepted before the LORD.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It is a sub-case: the offering is a burnt offering from the herd, one of the kinds named in the general rule
It is an oath
It is the main case, replacing the general rule
It is a wish
check.explain: Verse 2 states the general case with כִּי (a man who brings an offering). Verse 3 then takes up the burnt offering from the herd, introduced by אִם, the usual particle for a sub-case.

check.prompt: What is the condition in this law, and what is the answer?

quoted.title: Deuteronomy
quoted.english: If there be among you a needy man, one of thy brethren, within any of thy gates, in thy land which the LORD thy God giveth thee, thou shalt not harden thy heart, nor shut thy hand from thy needy brother;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The condition is 'if there is a needy man among you' (with כִּי); the answer is the prohibition 'do not harden your heart'
The condition is the land the LORD gives
The condition is 'you shall not harden your heart'; the answer is 'there is a needy man'
There is no condition; the verse is a wish
check.explain: כִּי־יִהְיֶה opens the case, 'if there is …', with a yiqtol. The answer is the commands that follow, introduced with לֹא תְאַמֵּץ.

check.prompt: What does וְאִם לֹא (words 4 and 5) do in the second half of this verse?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: If thou doest well, shall it not be lifted up? and if thou doest not well, sin coucheth at the door; and unto thee is its desire, but thou mayest rule over it.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It begins a question
It marks an oath, 'surely'
It sets the other half of a pair: 'and if you do not do well …'
It gives a wish
check.explain: The verse puts two conditions side by side, 'if you do well … and if you do not do well …'. This is a plain 'if not', not the oath form, because no oath has been sworn. The verse as a whole is hard to translate, but this pairing is clear.

check.prompt: How does the verse state the condition and the answer?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: If I ascend up into heaven, Thou art there; if I make my bed in the nether-world, behold, Thou art there.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The condition is a wish; the answer is a command
The condition has no particle; the answer is a qatal
The condition is אִם with a yiqtol, 'if I go up to heaven'; the answer is a clause with no verb, 'you are there'
There is no condition at all
check.explain: אִם־אֶסַּק supposes an act of the speaker. The answer, שָׁם אָתָּה, has no verb. The psalmist does not say that he goes up to heaven; he supposes it in order to say where God would be.

check.prompt: Which of these readings of אִם־אֶצְדָּק (words 0 and 1) is grammatically possible?

quoted.title: Job
quoted.english: Though I be righteous, mine own mouth shall condemn me; though I be innocent, He shall prove me perverse.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Only the oath sense 'I will not be righteous'
Neither: it must be a wish
Only 'because I am righteous'
Either an open condition, 'if I am right', or a concession, 'even if I am right'
check.explain: The yiqtol אֶצְדָּק after אִם can be read either way, and the verse makes sense both ways. There is no oath formula in the context, and nothing in the form requires a wish.

check.prompt: What does וְאִם לֹא הַגִּידוּ לִי (words 10 to 13) say?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And now if ye will deal kindly and truly with my master, tell me; and if not, tell me; that I may turn to the right hand, or to the left.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: 'If you had not told me'
'Surely tell me': an oath
'And if not, tell me': the alternative to the earlier אִם, with the same command repeated
'Because you do not tell me'
check.explain: The servant makes two suppositions: if they will deal kindly, tell him; and if not (if they will not), tell him as well. Both conditions lead to the same command, so that he may know which way to go.

reading.why: The opening laws of Exodus 21 show the pattern of the legal style: a main case introduced by כִּי and its sub-cases by אִם, with answers in yiqtol, weqatal and nominal clauses, and the new case at verse 7 begun by וְכִי.
